# SubKit

> A self-hosted engine for governed workflows. These pages describe setup, coding-agent briefings and hooks, the sk CLI, runtime settings, the connector catalog, and governed transactional email.
> All pages in one file: llms-full.txt

## Pages

- [What is SubKit?](llms/setup.md): SubKit runs recurring business tasks that span several systems and today depend on one person or a fragile script.
- [Use SubKit from a coding agent](llms/coding-agents.md): This chapter is for developers who work with Claude Code, Codex or Hermes.
- [sk CLI reference](llms/cli.md): Look up every sk command and argument here.
- [SubKit runtime settings](llms/settings.md): Look up every runtime setting with its description and default value.
- [Connector & recipe catalog](llms/connectors.md): Find the connector templates and recipes that ship with SubKit.
- [Reply by email to a signed request](llms/transactional-email.md): Someone sends a request through your form, for example for access, and should get a confirmation by email: exactly one, and only to their own address.

<!-- Source: setup.md -->

## What is SubKit?

SubKit runs recurring business tasks that span several systems and today depend on one person or a fragile script.
It is for teams that want such routine work to run reliably without writing software for it.
You describe the task in your own words, the AI drafts a workflow from it, and a person checks it and approves what it may touch.
After that it runs in fixed steps, with only the approved permissions.
Every run is recorded.

You work in the Cockpit in the browser, with the `sk` command line, or from AI clients such as Claude Code over MCP; the Web Clipper also collects web pages into your inbox.

![Overview with key figures for runs, success rate, connector health and cost, the "Needs you" list with open decisions and the latest failed runs](/docs-images/intro-overview.en.webp?v=8dfed08b2c2d)

The **Overview** shows at a glance what ran, what failed and what is waiting for your decision.
How to track cost and budget is in "Keep track of usage and costs".

Use it as SubKit Cloud or run your own engine:

- "Use SubKit Cloud": SubKit runs for you, and you sign in from the browser.
- "Run the engine": you run SubKit on your own server.

Then build your first workflow with "Your first workflow".

![Documentation page with search, the "Getting started" path with steps 1 to 4 and the "Working with SubKit" list](/docs-images/intro-docs.en.webp?v=85684f500db6)
## Use SubKit Cloud

> Cloud (hosted beta, by invitation)

With SubKit Cloud, SubKit runs for you. You install nothing and operate no engine of your own.
You sign in from the browser and work in the Cockpit of your workspace.

### What you need

- An invitation from a workspace administrator. There is no public sign-up.
- The address `https://subkit-cloud.mikebild.dev`. It takes you straight to the Cockpit.

### Get access

An administrator invites you from **People & access** > **Invite person**.
Sign-in, invitations and password emails go through Upraft Auth, the sign-in service of the platform SubKit Cloud runs on.

1. Open the email from "Upraft Auth".
2. Select the link and set a password.
3. Sign in as described in "Sign in".

Use the email address the invitation was sent to. A different address does not work.

### Sign in

1. Open `https://subkit-cloud.mikebild.dev`.
2. Select **Sign in with work account**.
3. Sign in at Upraft Auth with your email address and password.

The Cockpit opens in your workspace.
Your session ends after 8 hours of inactivity, or after 24 hours at the latest.

To build your first workflow, follow "Your first workflow".

### Switch accounts

Signing out in the Cockpit also signs you out at Upraft Auth.

1. In the Cockpit, select **Sign out**.
2. Sign in again with the other account.

### Switch workspaces

A workspace holds your workflows, connectors, knowledge, skills and runs.
People in one workspace cannot see another workspace.

1. In the Cockpit, select **Switch workspace**.
2. Select the workspace you want.

Workspaces you own are marked **Own** and show your role as **Owner**.
For the others, the list shows your role, such as Administrator or Member.

### Delete a workspace

> After 7 days, all workspace data is gone and cannot be restored.

Only the owner can delete a workspace.

1. In the Cockpit, open **Settings**.
2. Select **Delete workspace**.
3. Type the workspace name to confirm.
4. Select **Delete**.

What happens next:

- Access is suspended right away. Invited members lose their access.
- Sessions, API keys, invitations and MCP client connections are revoked.
- Your other workspaces are not affected.
- For 7 days you can change your mind. Sign in again and select **Reverse deletion**.

After you reverse a deletion, old keys and connections stay revoked.
Sign in again with the sk CLI and your MCP clients. Create a new key for the Web Clipper.

### Sign in with the sk CLI

The `sk` CLI signs in through the browser, like the Cockpit.

1. Install the CLI:

   ```bash
   curl -fsSL https://subkit-cloud.mikebild.dev/install | bash
   ```

2. Sign in. Use the address without `/cockpit`:

   ```bash
   sk login --engine-url https://subkit-cloud.mikebild.dev
   ```

3. In the browser that opens, select **Sign in with work account**.

The CLI then stores a personal key. Run `sk` to start.
For everything else, see "Use the sk CLI on your machine".

### Connect an MCP client

AI clients such as ChatGPT, Claude or Cursor can connect to SubKit Cloud over MCP.

1. In your client, add a remote MCP server with the address `https://subkit-cloud.mikebild.dev/mcp`.
2. In the browser sign-in that opens, select **Sign in with work account**.
3. On **Allow access**, select **Allow**.

You do not need to copy an API key. For more, see "Connect AI clients via MCP".

### Collect web pages

The Web Clipper collects web pages into the **Inbox**.
Set it up as described in "Collect web pages with the Web Clipper".
For SubKit Cloud, the engine address is `https://subkit-cloud.mikebild.dev`.

### What is different from self-hosting

SubKit Cloud runs the same engine as a self-hosted installation.
Some settings are managed by the operator instead of by you.

- **Models, budgets and limits.** The operator chooses them.
  You cannot add your own AI key or change these settings for your workspace.
- **Text models only.** Images, audio and other non-text input to the model are not supported.
- **No native web search.** The model's built-in web search is not available.
- **Public addresses only.** Connectors reach only services on the public internet.
  Addresses in a private network, such as `localhost` or an internal company server, are blocked.
- **Slack and Google Chat are locked.** Chat workspaces on these platforms stay locked
  until ownership of the workspace is verified. Use the chat in the Cockpit instead.
- **API keys for tools only.** API keys still work for the sk CLI, the Web Clipper, the HTTP API (Bearer)
  and MCP clients that use a key. Signing in to the browser with an API key exists only for
  self-hosted installations without an identity provider.
- **Export as a package.** You can export your own workflows, connectors, skills, schedules, knowledge sources and files as a package and import it into another engine.
  Credentials, approvals and run history are not included. See "Use the sk CLI on your machine".

### Limits and their messages

Every workspace has limits. The operator sets their values.
When you reach one, SubKit shows a message. Most of these messages appear in English; the table quotes them verbatim.

| What you see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| "Too many requests. Try again shortly." | You sent too many requests in a short time. Wait a moment and try again. |
| "The monthly request allowance is exhausted." | The month's request allowance is used up. Wait for the next month or contact the operator. |
| "The workspace storage allowance for files and saved content is exhausted. Retained content remains charged until physical cleanup succeeds." | Storage is full. Delete files and saved content you no longer need, or contact the operator. |
| "The workspace resource limit is exhausted. Ask the engine operator to review retained resources." | Too many resources. Delete workflows or connectors you no longer need, or contact the operator. |
| "This installation's monthly AI budget is used up." (in the chat) | Wait for the next month or contact the operator. |

### If something does not work

| What you see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| The invitation link or sign-in does not work | Use the email address the invitation was sent to. |
| You forgot your password | Upraft Auth sends you an email to reset it. |
| You want to use a different account | Follow "Switch accounts". |
| You are signed out unexpectedly | Your session ended after 8 hours of inactivity or 24 hours. Sign in again. |
| `sk login` or the MCP client cannot connect | Use `https://subkit-cloud.mikebild.dev` and `https://subkit-cloud.mikebild.dev/mcp`, without `/cockpit`. |
## Run the engine

Afterwards SubKit runs on your own server: the engine with the Cockpit, a PostgreSQL database and an object store, started with Docker Compose.
Database, files and keys stay on your server.

You need Docker with Compose, OpenSSL and a POSIX shell.
Put `docker-compose.yml` in a dedicated directory. Take it from the same published release as the engine image.
Use only published release images. If pulling the image fails, the installation is not finished, even if other services start.
Do not combine an older image with a newer Compose file.

Create the installation secrets once, before the first start. The command does not overwrite an existing `.env` and makes it readable only by its owner:

```bash
(
  set -eu
  umask 077
  set -C
  install_master_key=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
  install_database_password=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
  printf 'MASTER_KEY=%s\nSUBKIT_DB_PASSWORD=%s\n' \
    "$install_master_key" "$install_database_password" > .env
)
```

After the command succeeds, start the installation:

```bash
docker compose pull && docker compose up -d --wait
curl -fsS http://localhost:3000/health
```

Then set up the admin account and AI provider as described in "First-run setup".

### Protect keys and passwords

`MASTER_KEY` encrypts all stored secrets. If it is lost, those secrets can no longer be read.
Keep an encrypted backup of `.env` outside the installation directory.
Never regenerate `MASTER_KEY` for an existing database.

Also keep the database password unchanged when you reuse the database volume.
Changing `.env` does not change the password inside an already initialized PostgreSQL database.
Never commit `.env`. Do not share the output of `docker compose config` either, because it contains the secrets.

If you need to change `MASTER_KEY`, the offline command `--rewrap-master-key` re-encrypts the stored settings secrets with the new key.
It covers only these settings secrets. If other encrypted data exists, such as retained credentials, encrypted workflow or chat content, or approval proofs, it refuses.
In that case, keep the original `MASTER_KEY`.

The command runs only when all writing services have stopped.
You confirm this explicitly with `--all-producers-stopped` and back it with a separate file through `--stop-evidence-file`. Missing signs of life are not enough as proof.
If you run the database with a dedicated maintenance login, select it through the existing database configuration and pass `--maintenance`. That login receives only the designated maintenance functions.
The engine creates no database users.

### Start, stop and expose

For later starts, run `docker compose up -d --wait` from the same directory.
`docker compose stop` stops the services without deleting data.
The database and object store live in named volumes; `docker compose down -v` deletes them.
Keep the same Compose project name when you continue an installation.

At first, the API and database are reachable only over loopback, that is, only from the server itself.
Complete the first-run setup locally before you expose the API.
Access from outside needs HTTPS and access control. Never expose the database or object store publicly.

A recovery needs the database, object-store data, `.env`, the matching Compose file and the image identity together.
Test recovery in a separate installation before you rely on a backup or upgrade. The steps are under "Backup and recovery".

### Browser crawling for connector discovery

The supplied image contains no browser and no Node.js.
Connector discovery therefore looks for a service's documentation over HTTP: OpenAPI, GraphQL, Swagger UI, `llms.txt` and HTML pages.
When none of them finds the documentation, the result names the missing piece: "browser discovery is not available".
If the documentation needs JavaScript to display, provide a reachable OpenAPI specification or enter the connector endpoints yourself.

Browser crawling runs only when both conditions hold:

- `SK_PLAYWRIGHT_ENTRY` names an installed Playwright module with its Chromium build,
  readable by the container user (uid 1001), for example in your own image derived
  from the SubKit image.
- The outbound network guard is not strict. The container starts with `NODE_ENV=production`
  and therefore strict; it refuses browser discovery. The setting `egress.mode: permissive`
  also allows private and loopback addresses for every connector. Choose it only behind
  a network boundary you have reviewed.

A derived image is yours to maintain: keep Playwright and the browser updated, scan it
and ship the browser licenses. This path is not part of the release checks.

### Backup and recovery

A backup copies the whole installation and restores it with the same image.
To move only a workspace's own workflows, connectors, skills and knowledge to another engine, export a package instead, as described in "Use the sk CLI on your machine".

Plan a maintenance window for a consistent backup.
These steps apply to the bundled PostgreSQL and object store; external services need their own procedure.
Run the commands from the installation directory with its original Compose project name.
Create a new backup directory outside the installation directory, readable only by its owner, set `umask 077` and keep it encrypted.
The dump, object archive and `.env` contain sensitive data.

1. Record the running engine image identity with `docker inspect --format '{{.Image}}' "$(docker compose ps -q engine)"`.
   Preserve that image in a reachable registry or with `docker image save`, together
   with `docker-compose.yml` and `.env`. Do not rely on a mutable tag for recovery.
2. Stop writing services with `docker compose stop engine`. Back up PostgreSQL with
   `docker compose exec -T postgres pg_dump -U subkit -d subkit -Fc > /path/to/backup/postgres.dump`.
   Check the exit status before you continue. Keep the engine stopped until both data stores are backed up.
3. Stop the object store with `docker compose stop object-store`. Find its exact volume
   using `docker inspect --format '{{range .Mounts}}{{if eq .Destination "/data"}}{{.Name}}{{end}}{{end}}' "$(docker compose ps -aq object-store)"`.
   Archive it read-only with `docker run --rm --network none -v <object-volume>:/data:ro --entrypoint tar oven/bun:1.4.0-debian -C /data -cf - . > /path/to/backup/objects.tar`.
   Replace `<object-volume>` with that inspected name, not a guessed one.
4. Check that each command succeeded. Set all backup files to mode `0600` and record
   their SHA-256 checksums. Restart the original installation with `docker compose up -d --wait`.
   If a backup command fails, keep the original volumes and find the cause. An incomplete backup is not a recovery point.

Test recovery in a separate directory. Use `docker compose -p subkit-recovery` there for **every** Compose command below.
First check that this project name has no containers or volumes yet; otherwise choose another unused name.

Copy the saved Compose file and `.env` into it and keep `MASTER_KEY` and the database password.
Select the saved engine image with `SUBKIT_IMAGE` and set free loopback ports through `SUBKIT_HOST_PORT` and `SUBKIT_DB_PORT`.
Do not connect the test installation to external services that write data.

Starting the engine also starts its scheduler. Before the start, add a `docker-compose.override.yml` with this network isolation to the recovery directory.
Keep it in effect until you have reviewed restored schedules, triggers and connector permissions. Do not trigger real external effects through this project.

```yaml
networks:
  default:
    internal: true
```

1. Create fresh storage with `docker compose -p subkit-recovery create postgres object-store`.
   Inspect the new object-store container's `/data` volume as above, using the recovery
   project. Restore only into that new volume:
   `docker run --rm -i --network none -v <new-object-volume>:/data --entrypoint tar oven/bun:1.4.0-debian -C /data -xf - < /path/to/backup/objects.tar`.
2. Start the new database with `docker compose -p subkit-recovery up -d --wait postgres`.
   Restore it with `docker compose -p subkit-recovery exec -T postgres pg_restore --exit-on-error --clean --if-exists --no-owner -U subkit -d subkit < /path/to/backup/postgres.dump`.
   This command replaces database contents. Use it only against the new recovery project.
3. Start the recovered services with `docker compose -p subkit-recovery up -d --wait`.
   Check `/health` and `/ready` on the selected port and sign in with an existing account.
   Compare workflow records and downloaded file checksums, and verify an encrypted credential through a controlled test.
   A successful health check alone does not prove that the database, object files and key match.

This restores the same image and a consistent backup. It does not test an upgrade or a schema downgrade.
Data written after the backup is missing.
Keep the original installation until the recovery has been accepted.
## First-run setup

After this step your engine has an admin account, a first workspace and a verified AI provider, and you can sign in to the Cockpit.
The engine writes the one-time setup token to its log on first start; the command reads it from there.

```bash
docker compose exec engine sk init \
  --token "$(docker compose logs engine 2>&1 | grep -oE 'sk init --token [a-f0-9]{64}' | tail -1 | cut -d' ' -f4)" \
  --admin-email you@example.com \
  --tenant-name "My Org" \
  --llm-provider anthropic \
  --llm-api-key <your-provider-key>
```

Replace the email address, the name and the key with your own values.
`sk init` checks the key with one small test call before it saves anything.
If the provider refuses it, the setup stops and nothing is stored. The same token works for the next try.

Open the Cockpit at `http://localhost:3000/cockpit`.
If no sign-in provider is configured, sign in with an API key.
Then build your first workflow with "Your first workflow".

## Your first workflow

By the end of this chapter you have an approved workflow and a first run whose steps you can read.
You describe a task in the chat, save the workflow, approve it, start it and read the result.
It works the same in SubKit Cloud and on a self-hosted engine.

### What you need

- A SubKit account in a workspace.
  - Cloud: `https://subkit-cloud.mikebild.dev`
  - Self-hosted: `https://<your-engine>/cockpit`
- Permission to create and run workflows. Ask your administrator if a button is missing.
- An AI provider. Cloud provides one. A self-hosted engine uses the provider you chose in `sk init`.

### Sign in

1. Open the Cockpit.
2. Select **Sign in with work account**.

You land on **Overview** in your workspace.
Self-hosted without an identity provider? Select **Sign in with API key** instead and enter your key.

### Describe the task

1. In the navigation, open **Chat**.
2. Select **New conversation**.
3. Describe the task in your own words: what goes in, what should happen, what comes out.
   Example: "Fetch the open issues of my GitHub repository and give me a short list with title and link."
4. Answer the questions SubKit asks. If the task needs a service, SubKit asks you to connect it
   or to sign in to it.

Good to know: a small task is easier to check. You can extend the workflow later in the same chat.

### Save the workflow

When the workflow is ready, SubKit shows a card **Save workflow draft**.

1. Open **What will change** and read which steps and targets are included.
2. Select **Save inactive version**.

Saving starts nothing. The workflow now appears under **Workflows**.

Without the chat, you create a workflow under **Workflows** with **Create workflow**. The wizard guides you through **How**, **What**, **When** and **Check**.

### Approve what it may touch

A new version does not touch anything outside SubKit until a person approves it.
Without an approval, a run starts only as a trial run without effects.

1. Open **Workflows** and click your workflow. Its page opens on the **Overview** tab.
   The status line shows **Waiting for approval** or **Not approved**.
2. In the status line, select **Approve**.
3. Check **Environment**, **Validity** and **Operations and external targets**.
4. Confirm with **Approve**.
   **Apply only** applies the version without approving runs.

![Approval dialog for "Invoice export v1" with the environment "Test", the validity "Until revoked", one read on the Sales reporting API, no writes, and the "Apply only" and "Approve" buttons](/docs-images/first-workflow-approval.en.webp?v=a0dd838590e7)

Approving starts no run. It covers one environment and a duration.
A new version needs no new approval as long as it touches no more systems, addresses or write permissions than the approved one. If it reaches further, SubKit asks again and names the difference.
You can revoke it at any time in the **Approvals** tab.
If the chat offers an approval, it opens the same dialog.

| Field | What it controls |
| --- | --- |
| **Environment** | Where the runs are allowed, for example **Production**. |
| **Operations and external targets** | Which services and addresses the workflow reaches. Each service shows its provider's logo. |
| **Validity** | How long the approval applies: **7 days**, **30 days** or **Until revoked**. |

**When Approve is missing.** Some steps cannot be covered by any approval, for example a mail whose recipient comes from data, or a request with a free address. The status then reads **Change needed before approval** and names the step. Select **Fix it in the chat**: SubKit changes exactly those steps, checks them without live effects and saves a draft. Approve the new version afterwards.

### Start the workflow

1. On the workflow page, select **Start**.
2. Fill in the form if the workflow asks for inputs. You only type JSON under **Enter as JSON**.
3. Select **Start** to confirm. The dialog says **Starts a run of the approved version.**
   Without an approval, the button reads **Start a trial run**.

You see **Run started**. If the button is unavailable, the hint says why, for example
**Switch the workflow on before starting it.**

### Check the result

1. On the workflow page, open the **History** tab.
   The newest run is at the top, with its status. **Succeeded** means the run finished.
2. Click the run.
   You see every step with its output. A failed step shows **Error in step "…"** with the cause.

   ![Successful run of "CRM contact sync" with one "Query a service" step, the requester "API" and the collapsed "Why it was allowed" and "Technical details" sections](/docs-images/first-workflow-run-result.en.webp?v=d6f1c5541b42)

3. Optional: Select **In the audit trail** to see who started and approved the run.

### If something does not work

| What you see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| The run result is headed **Trial run result — not written** | The version has no approval yet. Follow "Approve what it may touch". |
| "Not started (…): no valid approval covers this run." | The approval is missing, expired or used up. Approve again or extend it. |
| "… must be reconnected" | Open the connector under **Connectors** and select **Sign in again**. |
| **You may not start this workflow.** | Ask your administrator for a role that may run workflows. |
| A step failed | Open the run, read the error and describe it in the same chat. SubKit suggests a fix that you review again. |

### The same in the terminal

With the `sk` command line you create workflows with `sk workflows create`, change them with `sk workflows update` and schedule them with `sk schedules create`.
If a step needs a change before approval, these commands report `automation: repair required`.
Check runs like this:

```bash
sk executions list --limit 5
sk executions steps <run-id>
sk executions result <run-id>
```

`sk workflows run <workflow-slug> --follow` starts another run and streams its steps.
For more, see "Use the sk CLI on your machine".
## Use the sk CLI on your machine

This chapter is for anyone who prefers the terminal or scripts to the Cockpit.
You install the `sk` command line, sign in and keep it up to date.
Afterwards you write workflows, connectors and knowledge as files and start runs from the terminal.

You get the `sk` command line straight from your engine. With it you draft, change and run workflows as files; `sk agent init` adds SubKit to Claude Code and Codex.
There is no npm package.

### What you need

- The address of your engine, without a path. The examples use `http://localhost:3000`.
  For SubKit Cloud, see "Use SubKit Cloud".
- Bash and curl.
- To sign in with an API key on a self-hosted engine: access to the engine host.

### Install and sign in

1. Install the CLI from your engine:

   ```bash
   curl -fsSL http://localhost:3000/install | bash
   ```

2. Sign in:

   ```bash
   sk login --engine-url http://localhost:3000
   ```

   Your browser opens. After you sign in, `sk` prints `sk: signed in as …` and saves the connection as a profile.
3. Run `sk`. Without a command it opens an interactive session; `sk --help` lists every command.

The engine also describes itself: the HTTP API at `/openapi.json`, the documentation for AI clients at `/llms.txt`.

### Sign in with an API key

Use this for scripts, or for a self-hosted engine without an identity provider.

1. On the engine host, issue an admin key. The command prints a ready `sk login` line:

   ```bash
   docker compose exec engine engine --issue-admin-key --tenant my-org
   ```

2. Run the printed line. It has this form:

   ```bash
   sk login --engine-url http://localhost:3000 --api-key <key>
   ```

   `sk` replies with `sk: profile 'default' saved` and the engine health.

### Work with several engines

A profile is a saved sign-in to one engine. It lets you work with a test and a production engine, or with several workspaces, without signing in again.
Profiles live in `~/.sk/config.json`.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `sk login --engine-url <address> --profile <name>` | Adds another profile. |
| `sk profile list` | Shows all profiles. |
| `sk profile use <name>` | Switches the active profile. |
| `sk status` | Shows the active profile and whether the engine is reachable. |
| `sk profile delete <name>` | Deletes a profile. |

For a single command, add `--profile <name>` without switching the active profile.

### Update the CLI

`sk update` installs the newest version, `sk update --check` only reports it.
`sk` fetches the version from the engine of your active profile first and only then from the public releases. You need no GitHub access for this.
Before replacing anything, `sk` verifies the signed checksums. If a file does not match, your current installation stays as it is.

The previous version is kept. `sk update --rollback` restores it.

### What the installers check

Each installer checks the files before it replaces an existing installation.
Missing license files, missing signatures or unsupported cryptography stop the installation.

| Installer | What it checks | What it trusts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/install` from the engine | The binary, `LICENSE` and `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt` against the checksum manifest of the engine or of an explicitly chosen mirror | The engine or mirror you chose, not a release signature |
| `sk update` | The signed checksum manifest of the release, then the binary and both license files | The pinned public release key, whether the files come from your engine or from GitHub |
| `scripts/install.sh` | The signed checksum manifest, then the binary and both license files | The pinned public release key |

### Install from a public release

Instead of your engine, you can also install `sk` from a signed public release.
The public beta is in preparation. Packages and the guide follow once released.

Once a release is published, check it out, review it and run `bash scripts/install.sh` in the checkout.
For this you also need OpenSSL with Ed25519 support on your PATH, for example OpenSSL 3.
The script installs the matching CLI for Linux or macOS and puts `subkit.LICENSE` and `subkit.THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt` next to it.
A local build or a private repository is not enough.

### Move your workspace to another engine

A package carries your own workflows, connectors, connector templates, skills, schedules, sources and their files to another engine.
Credentials, approvals, roles, categories, settings and the history stay behind.
To copy a whole self-hosted installation, make a backup instead, as described in "Run the engine".

You need `package:export` on the source engine and `package:import` on the target engine. Members and administrators have both.
After the import, someone with `credential:write`, usually an administrator, adds the credentials. A member can complete an OAuth sign-in.

1. Sign in to both engines, each with its own profile:

   ```bash
   sk login --engine-url https://<engine-a> --profile a
   sk login --engine-url https://<engine-b> --profile b
   ```

2. Export from engine A:

   ```bash
   sk packages export --out workspace.zip --profile a
   ```

   `--category <categories>` exports one area only, for example `--category devops,cloud`. Whatever the area needs comes along: connectors, connector templates, sub-workflows and schedules.
   `--only <kinds>` exports only some kinds. `--json` prints the result as JSON.
3. Import into engine B:

   ```bash
   sk packages import workspace.zip --profile b
   ```

   `sk` first shows the plan: each item is `create`, `update`, `unchanged` or `conflict`. Confirm it, or pass `--yes`.
   If engine B changed after the plan, the import stops and changes nothing. Then run it again.
4. Finish on engine B. Nothing runs or writes until you do:
   - Enter the credentials of each connector. The package contains none.
   - Activate the skills. They arrive as drafts.
   - Confirm the knowledge in the Cockpit review. It arrives as a proposal and is never admitted automatically.
   - Review the workflows and grant their approvals. They arrive as inactive drafts.
   - Resume the schedules. They arrive paused.
   - Start a test run.

Importing the same package again shows every item as `unchanged`.
An item you changed on engine B shows as `conflict` and is never overwritten.
`sk packages installs` lists past imports.

In the Cockpit you find the same in the "…" menu of workflows, connectors, skills, sources and files: "Export as package…" and "Import package…". If a category is filtered, the export already selects it.
In the chat, attach a package of up to 5 MB and ask to import it. The chat shows the plan and asks before importing, unless the conversation runs without confirmations. Import larger packages of up to 256 MB through the menu.

You can move area by area: one package per category, each with its preview, setup and test run.
A connector that an earlier package already brought stays `unchanged`, even after you stored its credentials on engine B.

### If something does not work

| What you see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| `sk: browser login failed` | The browser sign-in did not complete. Try again, or follow "Sign in with an API key". |
| `sk login` cannot reach the engine | Check the `--engine-url`. Give the address without a path. |
| A command lands on the wrong engine | Check the active profile with `sk status` and switch with `sk profile use <name>`. |
| `sk update` only asks GitHub or wants a GitHub token | Your CLI predates updating through the engine. Reinstall it once as in "Install and sign in". Updates then run through your engine. |
| `scripts/install.sh` stops with a missing license file or signature | Use a published public release. A local build or a private repository does not work. |
| `scripts/install.sh` stops because of unsupported cryptography | Put OpenSSL with Ed25519 support, for example OpenSSL 3, on your PATH. |
## Connect AI clients via MCP

This chapter is for anyone who wants to use SubKit from an AI client such as Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or Codex.
You register your engine there once as a server and sign in.
Afterwards the client finds and runs your workflows, with your permissions and with an entry in the history.

For Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and other AI clients, SubKit is an MCP server: every approved workflow is a tool there, plus connectors, knowledge and skills – with the permissions of the access, nothing beyond. Anything that writes waits for a person to choose "Allow once". The other way round, an MCP server you already use becomes a connector in SubKit; the operator decides per tool which of its tools run without asking.

### What you need

- The MCP address of your engine. Every engine has exactly one:

  ```text
  https://<your-engine>/mcp
  ```

  On SubKit Cloud it is `https://subkit-cloud.mikebild.dev/mcp`, always without `/cockpit`.
  Your own engine needs HTTPS. Plain HTTP works only on `localhost`.
- An account whose role allows MCP access. Without it, the sign-in ends with `access_denied`.
- An AI client that supports remote MCP servers over HTTP. If it can only start local servers, see "Connect with an API key".

### Choose how to sign in

| Way | When | What you do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Browser sign-in (OAuth)** | SubKit Cloud and engines with an identity provider | Enter the address. The client opens your browser, where you sign in and consent. In the cloud, select **Sign in with work account**. |
| **API key** | Clients that use a key, and engines without an identity provider | Enter a key in the client as a bearer token. |

Use the browser sign-in when you can. You copy no key, a consent page shows what the client may do, and the access renews itself.
An API key, by contrast, is long-lived access that sits on your machine.

### Connect with browser sign-in

1. In your client, add a remote MCP server with the address `https://<your-engine>/mcp` and name it `sk`.
2. In the browser window the client opens, sign in the same way as in the Cockpit.
3. On the page **Allow access**, check which client wants access to which workspace.
4. Check the boxes for what the client may do. **Read** is always on.
5. Select **Allow**. The browser returns to your client.

Where you add the server depends on the client:

- **claude.ai:** the settings for connectors. Add a custom connector with the address.
- **Claude Code:**

  ```bash
  claude mcp add --transport http --scope user sk https://<your-engine>/mcp
  ```

  Then run `/mcp` in Claude Code and select `sk` to sign in.
- **ChatGPT and Cursor:** the client's MCP or connector settings.

Menu names change between client versions. If a step looks different, follow your client's guide for remote MCP servers.

### Connect with an API key

1. In the Cockpit, open **API access** and create a key. The **Run** preset fits most clients.
2. Store the key in an environment variable, not in a file you share:

   ```bash
   export SK_API_KEY=<your-key>
   ```

3. Register the server in your client with the matching command.

Claude Code:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http --scope user sk https://<your-engine>/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer ${SK_API_KEY}"
```

Codex:

```bash
codex mcp add sk --url https://<your-engine>/mcp --bearer-token-env-var SK_API_KEY
```

Other clients send the header `Authorization: Bearer <your-key>` with every request.

If your client can only start local MCP servers, there is the command `sk mcp`. It uses your signed-in `sk` profile but offers only five tools: a connection check and four tools for conversations with SubKit. Your client reaches workflows, connectors and knowledge only through your engine's `/mcp` address.

A key without an MCP scope connects in **Read** mode.
If the client should also build, add `mcp:authoring` to `--scopes` when you create the key with `sk apikeys create`.

### Check the connection

1. Check that the engine answers:

   ```bash
   curl https://<your-engine>/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
   ```

   The answer names the MCP address and the scopes it offers:

   ```json
   {
     "resource": "https://<your-engine>/mcp",
     "authorization_servers": ["https://<your-engine>"],
     "scopes_supported": ["mcp:read", "mcp:authoring", "mcp:admin", "metrics:read"]
   }
   ```

2. In your client, ask: "Call the SubKit tool whoami." The answer names your account, your workspace and your scopes.
3. Ask: "Find a workflow in SubKit." The client calls `find_workflow` and lists what it finds.

If all three work, the client is connected.

### What the client may do

A scope is the level you give the client when it connects. It decides which tools the client sees at all.
Your role still limits every single call. A scope never gives the client more than you may do yourself.

| On the access page | Scope | The client can |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Read** | `mcp:read` | Read workflows, runs, connectors and knowledge, and run saved workflows. |
| **Authoring** | `mcp:authoring` | Additionally build workflows and connectors in a guided conversation. |
| **Administration** | `mcp:admin` | Additionally create, change and delete things in the workspace. |
| **Operational counters** | `metrics:read` | Read the operational counters, nothing else. |

- The access page only offers what your role allows.
- A key with `*` does not include authoring. That takes a deliberate `mcp:authoring`.
- An engine with `mcp.read_only` hides every write tool, even with `mcp:admin`.

### Read, run, write

- **Reads** run right away. Examples: `find_workflow`, `get_execution`, `search_knowledge`.
- **Runs** start a saved workflow, for example with `run_workflow` or a `wf_<slug>` tool.
  A short run answers right away. A long run answers with an `execution_id` that the client follows with `get_execution`.
- **Writes** change something: send an email, change data, change the workspace.
- **Packages** move your workspace's own resources to another engine with `export_tenant_package`, `preview_package_import` and `apply_package_import`.
  They ask for confirmation first. An import only creates drafts and proposals.

Writing always needs a person, in two places:

- **Writes inside a workflow:** A workflow writes for real only after a person approves it in the Cockpit. Without approval the run is a dry run: writes are held back and nothing is sent.
  A new version needs no new approval as long as it touches no more systems, addresses or write permissions than the approved one. If it reaches further, SubKit asks again and names the difference.
- **Write tools in the client:** A write tool pauses and returns a link.
  Open it, sign in, check what will happen, and select **Allow once** or **Decline**.
  Only then can the client finish the call with `confirm_tool_call`.

The AI cannot approve or allow anything itself. The link alone allows nothing either.

### Use an MCP server as a connector

The other direction: an MCP server your team already uses becomes a connector in SubKit. Workflows and the chat then call its tools.
Each tool asks before it runs, unless the operator has enabled it individually. Only someone allowed to change the connector can do that; a normal edit of the connector does not change this list.
`sk connectors mcp-inspect <id>` shows which tools the server actually offers. If the server needs OAuth client credentials, follow "External MCP OAuth credentials".

### If something does not work

The engine returns these messages in English; they are quoted verbatim here.

| What you see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| `401` with `missing_or_invalid_credentials` | Sign in again, or check the key and the `Authorization` header. |
| Sign-in ends with `access_denied` | Your role has no MCP permission. Ask an administrator for a role with MCP access. |
| `403` "Forbidden: invalid Origin header" | The request came from a foreign web page. Connect from the client, not from a web page, and use the engine's own address. |
| `403` `product_caller_forbidden` | The token belongs to an app user and has no MCP access. Use a person's sign-in or key. |
| `400` "Unsupported protocol version" | The client speaks an MCP version the engine does not know. Update the client. |
| `404` "Session not found" | The session expired, for example after an engine restart. Reconnect the server in the client. |
| Authoring tools are missing | The access has no `mcp:authoring`. Sign in again and check **Authoring**, or author with the sk CLI. |
| New tools are missing after an update | claude.ai keeps its old tool list. Remove the connector and add it again. |
## Use SubKit from a coding agent

This chapter is for developers who work with Claude Code, Codex or Hermes.
You give your agent the SubKit tools and, for each repository, a briefing from your team's shared knowledge.
Afterwards the agent runs approved workflows, knows the project's house rules and puts what it learned into your inbox for review.

### Why a coding agent plus SubKit

Your coding agent stays the tool for software: reading, changing and testing code.
Recurring business work needs more than a script: permissions, approvals, history, schedules and safely stored credentials. SubKit carries that.
To the agent, SubKit is a tool: it calls an approved workflow instead of holding credentials itself.
Every call goes through the same permission check as in the Cockpit and appears in the history.

Collected material always follows one path: **collect → review with your agent → confirm in the Cockpit → knowledge**.

### What you need

- The sk CLI, signed in to your engine. In the cloud, use `sk login --engine-url https://subkit-cloud.mikebild.dev` and **Sign in with work account**. The briefing uses this signed-in profile.
- The MCP address of your engine, `https://<your-engine>/mcp`. On SubKit Cloud it is `https://subkit-cloud.mikebild.dev/mcp`.
- Claude Code, Codex or Hermes.
- A repository where the briefings should appear.

### Set up the SubKit tools once per machine

1. In the Cockpit, open **API access** and create a key.
2. Store the key in `SK_API_KEY`.
3. Register SubKit in your client with the matching command.

Claude Code:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http --scope user sk https://<your-engine>/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer ${SK_API_KEY}"
```

Codex:

```bash
codex mcp add sk --url https://<your-engine>/mcp --bearer-token-env-var SK_API_KEY
```

A key without `mcp:authoring` lets the agent read and run workflows but build nothing. If it should draft workflows and connectors, create the key with `sk apikeys create --scopes …,mcp:authoring`.
To sign in without a key, see "Connect AI clients via MCP".

### Set up briefings in a repository

1. In the repository, declare the domains:

   ```bash
   sk agent init --domains <category>
   ```

   For several domains, separate them with commas: `--domains <category>[,<category>]`.
   The command writes `.sk/agent.json` and adds the SubKit hooks to `~/.claude/settings.json` and `~/.codex/hooks.json`. Other tools' hooks stay in place.
2. Commit `.sk/agent.json` so every checkout uses the same domains.
3. In Claude Code or Codex, run `/hooks` and check that the SubKit hooks are active.
4. Trust new or changed SubKit hooks.

### Set up Hermes by hand

For Hermes, `sk agent init` sets up no hooks. The command's output shows what you need under "Hermes (manual)".

1. In Hermes, register an MCP server over streamable HTTP with the address `https://<your-engine>/mcp`.
2. Pass the header `Authorization: Bearer ${SK_API_KEY}`.
3. At the start of a session, run `sk agent briefing` in the repository and hand the output to Hermes as context.

### Check the briefing

1. In the repository, run `sk status`.
2. Run `sk agent briefing --json`.
3. Check the fields `domains`, `knowledge_sources`, `skills_full` and `used_tokens`.

### Review collected material with your coding agent

Your agent can start a review of collected entries. You confirm the result in the Cockpit.

1. Ask your agent: "Review the new entries in Research. Which are useful? Propose what we should keep as knowledge."
2. Open the Cockpit link the agent returns. It leads to the item's **Review** tab.
3. Check the proposal's sources, exact text and knowledge destination.
4. Select **Confirm as source**.
5. Run `sk agent briefing --json` and check `knowledge_sources`.

A new session loads the updated briefing.

Good to know:

- Only a signed-in person with `intake:confirm` and `knowledge:write` confirms a proposal. An API key, an MCP client or the Web Clipper never does.
- The item's original stays linked to the knowledge it became.
- Moving, editing or discarding an entry never admits it as knowledge.

### Review collected material in the terminal

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `sk intake list` | Shows collected items in your default category. |
| `sk intake list --category research` | Shows collected items of one category. |
| `sk intake review --category research` | Starts the review and prints the Cockpit link. |
| `sk intake review --items <comma-separated-ids>` | Reviews only particular entries. |
| `sk intake default --category research` | Changes your personal default category. |
| `sk intake move --item <id> --category research` | Moves an entry to a category. |
| `sk intake discard --item <id>` | Discards an entry. |
| `sk intake restore --item <id>` | Restores a discarded entry. |

- Without a selection, `review` uses your default category.
- `--json` returns machine-readable results.
- These actions preserve the item's original and never admit knowledge.

### How briefings work

**Domains.** A domain is a catalog category or a `domain:<slug>` tag.

- `sk agent init` adds the requested domains and removes nothing that exists.
- Without `.sk/agent.json`, the hooks match the folder name against your project categories. On a unique match they create `.sk/agent.json` for you. Otherwise they ask instead of guessing.
- To fix the domains yourself, edit `domains` in `.sk/agent.json` and remove `inferred` and `inferred_folder_domain`.
- A prompt can add other matching domains as the task changes.

**Hooks.** `init` sets up the SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit and SessionEnd hooks for Claude Code and Codex. `--skip-claude` and `--skip-codex` leave that client's settings untouched.

**Size.** A briefing has at most 1,800 tokens and 9,500 characters, shared by both clients and the interactive sk session.
Whatever does not fit is shortened, and you see a warning.

A briefing contains:

- Domain context and a short status, with blocked work and deadlines first.
- Up to three specific next steps in your language.
- Matching sources and workflows of the folder's domain, named when they help with a task.
- The number of collected pages and session learnings, never their content. With `intake:read`, also the workspace-wide number of collected entries and pending proposals.

**Session learnings.** At session end, Claude Code and Codex send the transcript to the engine.

- The engine keeps only practices and facts a person taught or confirmed.
- It drops events, status updates and anything credential-related.
- The rest lands in the Inbox with origin `session`, in the project's shared category or your default category. A repeated learning adds evidence to the existing entry.
- Learnings are not knowledge and not skills until a person confirms them in the Cockpit. `sk intake list` shows what is waiting.

**Reviews with an agent.** The review runs in a saved SubKit conversation.

- MCP clients start it with `conversation_start`. `intake_item_ids` selects particular items and keeps that selection fixed.
- Tools that read entries or prepare proposals work only inside this conversation.
- For a new destination, include the topic category or `domain:<slug>` tag in the proposal. A changed proposal must be reviewed again.

### If something does not work

| What you see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| `sk agent briefing: no domains …` | There is no declaration. Pass `--domains` or run `sk agent init --domains <category>`. |
| `knowledge_sources` or `skills_full` are empty | The briefing works but nothing is assigned to the domain. Put knowledge and skills in the domain's category or use the `domain:<slug>` tag. |
| The client shows a briefing warning | The engine cannot be reached. The session continues. Check sign-in and connection with `sk status`. |
| No briefings in Claude Code or Codex | Open `/hooks`, check that the SubKit hooks are active, and trust new or changed hooks. |
| `/hooks` in Codex shows the SubKit hooks as disabled | Codex hooks are on by default, so no `config.toml` edit is normally needed. Check the effective feature setting and your administrator policy first, then follow the [Codex hooks guide](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks). |
| The agent cannot draft anything | Its key has no `mcp:authoring`. Create a new key with that scope. |
| The reminder about collected entries is missing | You lack the `intake:read` permission. Ask an administrator for it. |
| A proposal cannot be confirmed | Only a signed-in person with `intake:confirm` and `knowledge:write` can confirm, not an API key. Open the Cockpit link. |
## Collect web pages with the Web Clipper

This chapter is for anyone who collects material for their team while reading in the browser.
You install the Web Clipper, connect it to your engine and collect your first page.
Afterwards, whatever you find worth keeping lands in your Cockpit **Inbox** with its source and waits there for a review.

The Web Clipper is a Chrome extension. It drops a page, a selection or a YouTube transcript into your inbox as Markdown; it only becomes knowledge once a person confirms it. It is not in the Chrome Web Store yet; you set it up with `sk clipper install`.

The path is always the same: **collect → review in chat → confirm → knowledge or skill**.

### What you need

- **Google Chrome.** Microsoft Edge and other Chromium browsers are untested. Firefox is not supported, because the extension uses a Chrome background service worker.
- **An engine address** that uses HTTPS. Plain HTTP works only with `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]`. In SubKit Cloud it is `https://subkit-cloud.mikebild.dev`, without `/cockpit`.
- **An account with `intake:read` and `intake:write`.** If it lacks them, ask an administrator.
- **To install with the CLI:** the `sk` CLI, signed in to your engine. See "Use the sk CLI on your machine". Without the CLI, use the ZIP file.

### Install the extension

The installer copies your active profile's engine address into the extension. You only add an API key later.

1. Run `sk clipper install`. The command unpacks the extension to `~/.sk/clipper` and tries to open Chrome's extension page. The output names the folder and the next steps:

   ```text
   sk: clipping extension installed to /Users/you/.sk/clipper
   sk: in Chrome, enable Developer mode, select Load unpacked, and choose the directory above. Reload the extension there after a future install.
   ```

2. In Chrome, open `chrome://extensions`. If Chrome did not open by itself, the command prints `sk: could not open Chrome automatically`.
3. Turn on **Developer mode** (top right).
4. Select **Load unpacked** and choose the folder from the output.
5. Pin the "SubKit Clipper" extension to the toolbar.

The command has three options:

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--dir <directory>` | Installs to another folder. |
| `--engine-url <url>` | Uses this engine address instead of the active profile's. |
| `--no-open` | Does not open Chrome. |

### Install without the CLI

Your engine also offers the extension as a ZIP file. It contains no engine address; you enter it yourself when you connect.

1. Download `<engine address>/install/clipper.zip`, for example `https://subkit-cloud.mikebild.dev/install/clipper.zip`.
2. Unpack the file into a folder you keep. Chrome loads the extension from that folder.
3. In Chrome, open `chrome://extensions`, turn on **Developer mode** and select **Load unpacked** with the unpacked folder.

### Update the extension

After you update the `sk` CLI, install the Web Clipper again:

1. Run `sk clipper install`. If you used the ZIP file, unpack the new file into the same folder.
2. On `chrome://extensions`, reload the "SubKit Clipper" extension.

The engine address and language stay. Paste the API key again after the reload.

### Connect it to your engine

The Web Clipper signs in with its own API key.

1. In the Cockpit, open **API access**.
2. Select **Create key** and pick the **Web Clipper** preset. It grants exactly `intake:read` and `intake:write`.

   !["Create key" dialog with the Web Clipper preset, which grants only View and Edit on collected items](/docs-images/web-clipper-api-key.en.webp?v=d37e5c477602)

3. Copy the key and keep it in a password manager.
4. In the Web Clipper, select the gear icon (⚙). The settings open in a new tab.
5. Check the **Engine address** and paste the key into **API key**.
6. Select **Save connection**.
7. Allow access when Chrome asks for it.

The Web Clipper checks the connection, loads your categories and confirms that the key may save items.
After a browser restart, paste the key again; "Privacy" explains why.

If the engine address changes, you need the key for the new engine. **Clear API key** removes the key from the extension.

### Collect a page

1. In the toolbar, select the "SubKit Clipper" icon.
2. Check the **Title**.
3. Optional: fill in **Why is this interesting?**.
4. Pick a **Category**, or select **New category**. Names use lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, up to 40 characters.
5. Check the preview.
6. Optional: open **Details and edit content** to see author and date and to edit the Markdown.
7. Select **Collect**.

It is quicker to right-click and select **Save page to SubKit** or **Save selection to SubKit**, or to press **Alt+Shift+K**. Change the shortcut at `chrome://extensions/shortcuts`.

On success, the popup says for example "Collected: research. Not yet admitted as knowledge or a skill." **Review in chat** starts the review right away.
If saving fails, your draft stays in the Web Clipper. The same page is never collected twice.

### What happens next

1. **Inbox:** in the Cockpit, open **Inbox** and click the item. On its page you read, edit or discard it.
2. **Review:** select **Review in chat** in the Web Clipper or in the item's menu. The chat prepares a proposal: the exact content, its sources and the destination (knowledge or skill).
3. **Confirm:** a person signed in to the Cockpit in the browser confirms the proposal on the item's **Review** tab as a source or skill.

To confirm, that person needs `intake:confirm` and the right of the destination:

| Destination | Needed rights |
| --- | --- |
| Knowledge | `knowledge:write` |
| Skill | `skill:write` and `skill:activate` |
| Skill that replaces others | also `skill:archive` for each replaced skill |

API keys, MCP clients and the Web Clipper itself cannot confirm.
Until it is confirmed, an item is not knowledge, and ordinary knowledge search does not find it. Moving or editing it changes nothing about that; if the proposal changes, you review it again.
More in the chapter "Collect ideas and turn them into knowledge or skills".

### What the Web Clipper captures

- **A page:** the main article text as Markdown, links as absolute addresses, without navigation and recommendations.
- **A selection:** only the selected text. From the toolbar or the shortcut, the Web Clipper uses your selection if there is one, otherwise the whole article.
- **A YouTube video:** title, author, publish date, description and the transcript in the original audio language. Include or exclude description and transcript under **Details and edit content**.

It also keeps the source address, author and publish date when the page provides them. Image links stay in the text; the Web Clipper uploads no image files and no screenshots.

### Privacy

- **Destination:** items go only to the engine you configured. For a transcript, the Web Clipper may also load the page and captions directly from YouTube.
- **Credentials are redacted:** before saving, SubKit replaces recognizable credentials (API keys, tokens, private keys, signed-link signatures) with a marker. The values are never stored. Personal data is kept, so don't clip pages that show passwords or keys.
- **Your API key** sits only in the browser's session storage and is never written to your device. That is why you paste it again after a browser restart or a reload of the extension. A key from the **Web Clipper** preset only views and edits collected items (`intake:read`, `intake:write`), including other people's clips in this workspace. Revoke it in the Cockpit when you no longer need it.
- **What the key can reach:** the **Web Clipper** preset grants only viewing and editing collected items (`intake:read`, `intake:write`), including other people's clips in your workspace. Revoke the key in the Cockpit when you no longer need it.
- **Originals stay:** the engine keeps the original captured snapshot. Later edits do not overwrite it, and the item stays linked to the knowledge or skill made from it.
- **Visibility:** items follow the permissions of your workspace. Categories are shared, not private.

### If something does not work

The Web Clipper shows messages in the selected language. **Help** in the popup and in the settings opens this chapter on your engine.
If a capture from the context menu or the shortcut fails, the Web Clipper opens its popup in a tab and shows the error there.

#### Connection and key

| What you see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| "Set an engine address and API key first. …" or "Set an engine address before capturing." | Enter both in the settings (⚙) and save. After a browser restart, paste the key again. |
| "The API key is invalid or expired. …" | Create a new key with the **Web Clipper** preset under **API access** and save it in the settings. |
| "The API key lacks intake:read. …" or "… lacks intake:write. …" | Create a key with the **Web Clipper** preset under **API access**. Your draft stays. |
| "The SubKit API could not be reached. …" | Check the engine address, your internet connection and whether Chrome may access the address. |
| "Use an HTTPS address or HTTP on localhost." | Use `https://`, or `http://` only with `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]`. The address must not contain a user name, a password, a `?query` or a `#fragment`. |
| "Allow access to this engine to save the connection." | Save again and allow access when Chrome asks. |
| "Enter an API key for the new engine." | You changed the engine address. Paste the key for the new engine. |
| "Categories currently unavailable" | Select **Check connection**. |

#### Capturing

| What you see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| "The main content could not be captured reliably. …" | Select the relevant text, then select **Capture again**. |
| "The content was captured as simplified text. …" | Check in the preview that everything is there. |
| "No text was captured. …" | Select **Capture again**. For an excerpt, select the text first. |
| "No transcript is available." | The Web Clipper could not read a transcript for this video. |
| "Open the clipper from the toolbar on this page again." | Chrome needs access to this site. Select the toolbar icon on that page. |
| "The page changed while it was being captured. Capture it again." | Capture again. |
| "The page could not be captured." | Reload the page and try again. |

#### Collecting

| What you see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| "Saving is not confirmed yet. Retry; your draft remains available." | The network or the engine failed. Select **Try again**. |
| "SubKit rejected the clip. …" | Check the category and the content, then try again. |
| "This clip already exists." | It was already collected. |
| "Choose a valid category before collecting." or "Enter a valid category." | Use lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, at most 40 characters. |
| "The saved category is unavailable. Choose another category." | Pick another category. |
| "This draft belongs to a different engine." | Switch back to the engine it was made for to send it. |
## Collect ideas and turn them into knowledge or skills

This chapter is for anyone who wants to keep web pages, notes or learnings from AI sessions without deciding right away. Everything lands in the Cockpit under **Inbox**. It only becomes knowledge or a skill once a signed-in person with write rights confirms it in the Cockpit.

The path is always the same: **collect → review in chat → confirm → knowledge or skill**.

### What you need

- For web pages: the Web Clipper in Chrome, installed and connected. How to set it up is in the chapter "Collect web pages with the Web Clipper".
- To collect: an account with `intake:read` and `intake:write`.
- To confirm: a Cockpit sign-in with `intake:confirm`. Add `knowledge:write` for knowledge, or `skill:write` and `skill:activate` for a skill. Replacing skills also needs `skill:archive` for each replaced skill.

### Collect something

The **Inbox** collects from two directions:

- **Web pages** from the Web Clipper. They carry the origin **Browser**.
- **Learnings from sessions** with AI assistants. Their origin names the assistant, such as **Claude Code**, **Codex** or **Chat**. When it is unknown, it reads **AI assistant**.

To collect a web page:

1. Open the page in Chrome.
2. Optional: select the text you want as an excerpt.
3. In the toolbar, select the Web Clipper icon ("SubKit Clipper").
4. Check the preview. The source address is captured automatically.
5. Optional: add why the page matters.
6. Pick a category. Your default category is preselected, at first `inbox`.
7. Select **Collect**.

### Add a note

A note is an item without a source address, such as a thought or an idea.

1. In the Cockpit, open **Inbox** and select **Add entry**. If the Inbox is still empty, select **Add a note**.
2. In the **Add to intake** dialog, enter a **Title**.
3. Write the text under **Content**. Markdown is allowed.
4. Pick a **Category**, or create one with **New category…**.
5. Select **Add**.

The note carries the origin **Note**. It has no **Open original page** link, because there is no source.

### Review and organize items

1. In the Cockpit, open **Inbox**.

   ![Inbox with seven collected items of origin "Note", "Browser", "Claude Code", "Chat" and "Codex" in category Inbox, status "Collected", and the hint that three entries from your AI assistants are waiting for your review](/docs-images/collect-ideas-and-turn-them-into-knowledge-or-skills-inbox.en.webp?v=147e1f8a806b)

2. Optional: above the list, click the hint, for example "3 entries from your AI assistants are waiting for your review". You then only see items from your AI assistants. The filter **Origin: AI assistant** appears next to the search; click it to clear it.
3. Click an item. On the **Content** tab, one sentence names the origin, such as "Collected by Chat in the session … · for … · …". **Open conversation** takes you to the chat conversation, **Open original page** to the collected page.
4. Optional: select **Edit item** to change title, content or category. The captured original is preserved.
5. Optional: select **Discard** or **Restore**.

Who sees what in the Inbox follows the permissions of your workspace. Categories are not private.

### Review in chat

To review one item:

1. In the **Inbox**, open the item.
2. Select **Review in chat**. The chat shows the item as an `@` reference.

For a whole category, start the category's review suggestion in a new chat. Or ask: "Look through my new Research entries and suggest what to keep."

The chat prepares a proposal with content, sources and destination, and links to it. The link opens the item's **Review** tab. Completed decisions appear on the **History** tab under **Proposals and decisions**.

### Confirm a proposal

Only a person who is signed in to the Cockpit and has `intake:confirm` plus the right for the destination can confirm. API keys, MCP clients and the Web Clipper cannot confirm.

1. Open the item and select **Review**.
2. Read the proposal: content, sources and destination.
3. Select **Confirm as source** or **Confirm as skill**.

Only now does knowledge search find the result, and only now do agent briefings carry the skill. If a skill replaces other skills, confirming archives them. The proposal shows each of these changes beforehand.

Good to know:

- Moving, editing or discarding an item never makes it knowledge.
- If a proposal or one of its sources changes, you review it again.
- SubKit replaces credentials such as API keys and tokens before an item is saved.
- The item's original stays linked to the knowledge or skill.
- How to keep maintaining confirmed sources and skills is in the chapter "Maintain sources, skills and files".

### If something does not work

| What you see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| The Web Clipper reports no connection or an invalid key | Follow "If something does not work" in the chapter "Collect web pages with the Web Clipper". |
| An item is missing in the **Inbox** | Check the category and the origin. Clear the **Origin** filter. |
| "You lack the rights for this. …" | Ask an administrator for `intake:confirm` and the right for the destination. |
| "This suggestion changed. Review the current content before confirming it." | Read the current content, then confirm again. |
| "A skill this suggestion refers to can no longer be loaded. …" | Revise the suggestion in the chat before you confirm. |
## Use the HTTP API

Your program, script or backend should start an approved workflow and keep working with its result.
This chapter is for developers and takes you from the first key to a run you have read.
Afterwards you know how to start runs, wait for them and handle errors cleanly.

Every example uses `curl`, so you can try it in a terminal first.
SubKit Cloud and a self-hosted engine behave the same here.

### What you need

- Your engine address.
  - Cloud: `https://subkit-cloud.mikebild.dev` (without `/cockpit`)
  - Self-hosted: `https://<your-engine>`
- An API key with the scopes `workflow:read`, `workflow:run` and `execution:read`. A scope is a single permission the key carries. Create the key with the sk CLI, as shown below, or in the Cockpit under **API access**. For the CLI, sign in as described in "Use the sk CLI on your machine".
- A workflow that is active and approved. See "Your first workflow".
- `curl` in your terminal.

### Reach the engine

`/health` needs no key.

1. Set the address as a variable:

   ```bash
   export SK_URL=https://<your-engine>
   ```

2. Call `/health`:

   ```bash
   curl -s "$SK_URL/health"
   ```

   ```json
   { "status": "ok", "service": "subkit", "version": "<version>" }
   ```

### Create and check an API key

1. Create a key with exactly the permissions this chapter needs:

   ```bash
   sk apikeys create --name http-api-test --scopes workflow:read,workflow:run,execution:read
   ```

2. Copy `plaintext_key` from the JSON response. It is shown only once, so keep it in a password manager.
3. Put the key in a variable:

   ```bash
   export SK_KEY=<api-key>
   ```

4. Ask the engine who you are:

   ```bash
   curl -s "$SK_URL/v1/identity/whoami" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $SK_KEY"
   ```

   The answer names your account, your workspace and the key's scopes (shortened). The workspace is your team's separate area in the engine:

   ```json
   {
     "id": "<user-id>",
     "kind": "user",
     "tenant_slug": "<workspace>",
     "role_name": "admin",
     "scopes": ["workflow:read", "workflow:run", "execution:read"]
   }
   ```

Without `--scopes`, the key gets the same scopes as your own access.
`sk apikeys revoke <key-id>` revokes the key.

### List your workflows

1. Fetch the active workflows:

   ```bash
   curl -s "$SK_URL/v1/workflows?status=active&limit=20" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $SK_KEY"
   ```

   Each entry in `items` carries, among others, `id`, `slug`, `name`, `lifecycle` and `operating_status`. In the example the workflow is called "Daily report" (shortened):

   ```json
   {
     "items": [
       {
         "id": "<workflow-id>",
         "slug": "daily-report",
         "name": "Daily report",
         "lifecycle": "active",
         "operating_status": "active"
       }
     ],
     "total": 1,
     "categories": [{ "category": "reporting", "count": 1 }]
   }
   ```

2. Copy the `id`. A run needs the ID; the engine does not accept a slug.

`q=<text>` searches name, slug, description and category.

### Start a run

- Send the workflow ID and its input to `/v1/executions`:

  ```bash
  curl -s -X POST "$SK_URL/v1/executions" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $SK_KEY" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"source":"saved","workflow_id":"<workflow-id>","input":{}}'
  ```

  The call waits for the run and answers `200` with `execution_id`, `status`, `output` and `steps`.

`input` must match the workflow's input. `GET /v1/workflows/<workflow-id>/input-schema` shows what it expects.

### Start a long run in the background

1. Send the run with `"async":true`. Optionally add an `Idempotency-Key` header. With it, a call sent twice by accident still starts only one run:

   ```bash
   curl -s -X POST "$SK_URL/v1/executions" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $SK_KEY" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -H "Idempotency-Key: daily-report-<date>" \
     -d '{"source":"saved","workflow_id":"<workflow-id>","input":{},"async":true}'
   ```

   The engine answers `202` right away:

   ```json
   { "execution_id": "<execution-id>", "status": "queued", "hold_writes": false }
   ```

2. Copy `execution_id` and read the result as described in the next section.

- The `Idempotency-Key` header takes 1 to 200 characters.
- If you send the same key again, no second run starts. The answer carries the first run's ID and `"idempotent_replay": true`.

### Read the result

1. Read the run:

   ```bash
   curl -s "$SK_URL/v1/executions/<execution-id>" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $SK_KEY"
   ```

2. Check `status`.
3. On a failure, read `outcome.failed_step` for the step and `error` for the cause.
4. Read each step's output:

   ```bash
   curl -s "$SK_URL/v1/executions/<execution-id>/steps" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $SK_KEY"
   ```

   Each entry has `step_key`, `status` and a preview in `output_preview` or `result_preview`. The last step usually holds the workflow's result.

| `status` | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `queued`, `running` | The run is still working. |
| `succeeded` | The run is done. |
| `failed`, `timed_out`, `aborted` | The run stopped early. |

`outcome.kind` summarizes the run, for example `succeeded`, `failed` or `held`.
`sk executions result <execution-id>` shows the same result in your terminal.

### Check whether a workflow can run automatically

Before a workflow runs on a schedule, you want to know whether an approval can cover it at all. The field `automation_readiness` holds that answer.

You get it when you save a workflow (`POST /v1/workflows`, `PUT /v1/workflows/{id}`). You also get it when you create or change a schedule (`POST /v1/schedules`, `PUT /v1/schedules/{id}`). The field has the shape `{environment, workflow_version_id, state, issues, repair_guidance}`.

| `state` | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `eligible` | A person can approve recurring runs. |
| `repair_required` | No approval can cover the named steps until they change. |
| `verification_unavailable` | The engine could not run the check. Try again later. |

Each `issues` entry names a `step_id` and a `code`. `repair_guidance` says how to change that step. A paused schedule gets no verdict.

### Export and import a package

A package moves your workspace's own resources to another engine. The steps after the import are in "Use the sk CLI on your machine".
Export needs `package:export`, import needs `package:import`.

| Route | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /v1/packages/export` | Creates the package and answers with its `file_id`. |
| `GET /v1/packages/archives/{file_id}` | Downloads the package as a zip file. |
| `POST /v1/packages/import/preview` | Takes the zip as multipart field `archive`, or `{"archive_file_id": "<file-id>"}`. Answers with a plan per item and a `plan_digest`. Changes nothing. |
| `POST /v1/packages/import/apply` | Takes `{"archive_file_id": "<file-id>", "expected_plan_digest": "<plan-digest>"}` and applies the plan. |
| `GET /v1/packages/installs`, `GET /v1/packages/installs/{id}` | Lists past imports. |

If the target changed after the preview, apply answers `409`. Run the preview again.

### Page through lists

Lists return one page at a time. `total` counts all matches.

| List | Page size | Next page |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /v1/workflows` | `limit` (up to 200) | `offset`: skip that many entries |
| `GET /v1/executions` | `limit` (up to 200) | `cursor`: the previous page's `next_cursor` |

Runs come newest first. Pass `next_cursor` back exactly as you received it. When it is `null`, you are on the last page.

```bash
curl -s "$SK_URL/v1/executions?workflow_id=<workflow-id>&status=failed,timed_out&limit=50" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SK_KEY"
```

`status` takes several values, separated by commas.

### How the API is organized

- Every route starts with `/v1`, for example `/v1/workflows`.
- You send your API key in the `Authorization` header as `Bearer <api-key>`. "Bearer" means: whoever presents the key counts as authorized.
- Requests and responses are JSON.
- `/openapi.json` describes every route, field and status code in OpenAPI format.
- `/docs` shows the same description as a searchable reference. Open `https://<your-engine>/docs` in a browser.

### Errors and status codes

Errors are JSON with a machine-readable `code` and a readable `message`:

```json
{
  "code": "not_found",
  "message": "workflow not found",
  "trace_id": "<trace-id>"
}
```

Some errors add `hint` (what to do), `details` (for example the invalid fields) or `retry_after` (seconds).
Branch on `code` in your program, not on `message`. Keep `trace_id` when you report a problem.

| Status | `code` (examples) | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `200` | | Done. |
| `202` | | Accepted. The run continues in the background. |
| `400` | `bad_request` | The request is invalid. `details` names the fields. |
| `401` | `unauthorized` | The key is missing, wrong, expired or revoked. Check `Authorization: Bearer <api-key>`, or create a new key. |
| `403` | `forbidden` | The key lacks a scope or your role lacks the permission. Create a key with `workflow:read`, `workflow:run` and `execution:read`. |
| `404` | `not_found` | The ID does not exist in your workspace. |
| `409` | `conflict` | The current state does not allow it. For a run: there is no active version, or the approval is missing or used up. |
| `429` | `rate_limit_exceeded`, `rate_limited` | A limit is reached. Wait as long as the `Retry-After` header says. Then retry with the same `Idempotency-Key`. |
| `500` | `internal_error` | An error in the engine. Report the `trace_id`. |

### If something does not work

| What you see | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| `404 Not Found` as plain text | The path does not exist. Check that it starts with `/v1`. |
| `400` with `request validation failed` | Read `details`. Often `workflow_id` is not a UUID or `input` does not match the input schema. |
| The run answers with `"hold_writes": true` | The version has no approval for this environment. Nothing was written. Approve it as described in "Your first workflow". |
| Any other error status | Look up the status in "Errors and status codes" and read `message` and `details`. |
## Onboard an app

Your app signs its users in at its own identity provider and should start SubKit workflows on their behalf.
This checklist is for developers who set up that connection.
At the end, the app calls SubKit with its users' tokens and needs only the product ID and the workflow IDs.

The identity provider is the service your users sign in at.
After sign-in it issues an access token, a signed and time-limited proof of who the person is.
The app sends this token to SubKit as a bearer token in the `Authorization` header.
SubKit checks the token's signature, issuer and audience before a run starts.

Work through the steps in order.
Hosts and IDs in the examples are placeholders (`example.test`, `<...>`).

### What you need

- The `sk` CLI, signed in to your engine. In SubKit Cloud the engine address is `https://subkit-cloud.mikebild.dev`, without `/cockpit`.
- A real access token of a test account of the app.
- Access to the services the workflows call, such as your AI model's API.

### 1. Choose the product ID and sign-in rules

Pick these values before you change any setting.
A claim is a field in the token, such as `iss` (who issued it) or `aud` (who it is meant for).
Read both from a real token of the app.

| Setting | What to enter | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `product_id` | A lowercase name (`^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,62}$`), one per app. It ties provider, workflows, budget and identity binding together. | `<product-id>` |
| `issuer_url` | The provider's issuer, exactly as in the token's `iss` claim. HTTPS outside localhost. | `https://idp.example.test` |
| `audience` | Who the token is meant for: the value of the `aud` claim. The issuer defines it; SubKit has no default. | `<audience>` |
| `required_claims` | Who may sign in: a dot path into the verified token with an exact value. The key is required. | `[{"path":"idp","equals":"primary"}]` |

The first verified token of a person creates a product user with the built-in member role.
An empty `required_claims` list `[]` admits every token of that issuer and audience.
If not every person with a token should become a user, narrow `required_claims` to the intended accounts.

### 2. Set the runtime configuration

The runtime configuration is your engine's settings, which you read and write with `sk settings`.
`auth.providers` and `products` are each replaced as a whole.
So read each value first and write it back with your addition.

1. Read the current sign-in providers.

```bash
sk settings get auth.providers --json
```

2. Add your provider entry and write the whole list back. Keep every existing entry, or it is lost.

```bash
sk settings set auth.providers '[
  {"protocol":"api_key","id":"api-key","label":"SubKit API key"},
  {"protocol":"oidc_bearer","id":"<provider-id>","label":"<app> account",
   "issuer_url":"https://idp.example.test","audience":"<audience>","algorithms":["ES256"],
   "product_id":"<product-id>","tenant_slug":"default",
   "required_claims":[{"path":"idp","equals":"primary"}],
   "reject_anonymous":true,"clock_tolerance_s":30}
]'
```
